title: Ten Years After Kattappa Killed Baahubali, Netflix Opens the Gates of Mahishmati Again — This Time There's No Script
excerpt: 'Baahubali: The Torchbearer' lands worldwide on June 26 — the docu-series that finally lets you behind the curtain of the film that taught Indian cinema to dream in IMAX.
body:
It started with a question that became a national obsession: Why did Kattappa kill Baahubali? For an entire year, India argued about it at dinner tables, in WhatsApp groups, in office corridors from Hyderabad to Houston. Now, ten years after Prabhas first walked up that waterfall and refused to come back down, Netflix is handing fans the keys to the kingdom — and this time, there's no screenplay protecting the magic.

https://x.com/NetflixIndia/status/2070009089904570542

Baahubali: The Torchbearer, a documentary series celebrating a decade of the franchise that rewrote the rules of Indian filmmaking, drops worldwide on Netflix on June 26, 2026. It is, quite literally, a homecoming. For the generation that lived through the two-year wait between The Beginning (2015) and The Conclusion (2017), this is a chance to relive the fever. For everyone who came later, it's an invitation into Mahishmati through the front gate.

**"Can't wait for the world to see it." — Prabhas

That quote was about the franchise's animated future, but it doubles neatly as the spirit of the whole anniversary moment."**

And what a gate it is. The docu-series goes behind the legend to unpack how S. S. Rajamouli — a director from Hyderabad with what colleagues called a "seemingly impossible ambition" — convinced an industry, and then a planet, that a Telugu period epic could stand shoulder to shoulder with anything Hollywood put on a screen. The making of those colossal battle sequences. The world-building of an entire fictional empire. The cultural earthquake that followed. It's all here.

!The Torchbearer — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

"The team is building something truly special. Can't wait for the world to see it." — Prabhas

That quote was about the franchise's animated future, but it doubles neatly as the spirit of the whole anniversary moment. Because The Torchbearer isn't arriving in a vacuum. It's the centrepiece of a Baahubali year that refuses to let the saga rest. Last October, Rajamouli personally re-edited both films into a single 225-minute Telugu cut — Baahubali: The Epic — remastered MM Keeravani's thunderous score, slipped in a previously unreleased scene, and sent the whole thing back into IMAX, 4DX and Dolby Cinema. It was a bold experiment, and audiences showed up like it was 2017 all over again.

Then there's what comes next. Baahubali: The Eternal War, a two-part 3D animated saga in which the murdered prince Amarendra is pulled into a cosmic battle between Devas and Asuras across fourteen mystical realms, was just showcased in the Work in Progress section at the Annecy International Animation Film Festival — the Cannes of animation. Directed by Ishan Shukla, backed by Arka Media Works at a reported ₹120 crore, with Prabhas and Ramya Krishnan returning to voice their characters and Keeravani back on the music, it targets a 2027 release. Rajamouli has been careful to clarify: this is not Baahubali 3. It's a new dimension of the same universe.

Which is exactly why The Torchbearer matters. It's the connective tissue — the story of how an idea born in a Hyderabad writing room became a graphic novel, two animated series, a trilogy of English novels, a re-release phenomenon, and now an animated epic with global festival pedigree. Few film franchises anywhere have this kind of cultural afterlife. Marvel had to assemble an army of studios to build a universe. Rajamouli more or less did it from one fixed point of pure conviction.

For the diaspora, the timing is a gift. The Torchbearer streams on Netflix worldwide from June 26 — no region-locking, no "available in select territories," no hunting for a grainy stream. Whether you're in New Jersey, London, Toronto or Melbourne, it lands on your home screen the same day it lands in India. And for NRI parents who've spent years trying to explain to skeptical kids why Baahubali is a big deal, here's the proof, in HD, with the people who built it doing the talking.

The Baahubali magic was always about scale — armies, waterfalls, a golden throne, a question that held a billion people hostage for a year. The Torchbearer finally turns the camera the other way, onto the dreamers who pulled it off. Ten years on, the throne of Mahishmati is still the most coveted seat in Indian cinema. This week, you get to see how it was built.
